lesson.title: Writing the Verdict: How to State a Hypothesis Test Conclusion
lesson.summary: A complete hypothesis test conclusion compares the p-value to alpha, states the formal decision about H0, and restates that decision in the context of the original question, without ever claiming to have proven anything.
lesson.body:
A complete conclusion has three parts. First, compare: state the p-value against alpha explicitly, such as "because p equals some value, which is less than (or not less than) alpha equals some value." Second, decide: state the formal decision, "we reject H0" or "we fail to reject H0." Third, contextualize: restate what that decision means in terms of the real-world question, using the actual variables and units from the problem rather than stopping at symbols.

For the cereal box test at alpha = 0.05, a full conclusion reads: "Because the p-value of 0.0456 is less than alpha equals 0.05, we reject H0. There is convincing evidence that the true mean fill weight of cereal boxes differs from the claimed 16 ounces." Now contrast that with alpha = 0.01: "Because the p-value of 0.0456 is not less than alpha equals 0.01, we fail to reject H0. There is not convincing evidence, at this stricter standard, that the true mean fill weight differs from 16 ounces." Both conclusions use the exact same data and the exact same p-value, only the pre-chosen standard changed, which is precisely why choosing alpha in advance and reporting it honestly matters so much.

Certain phrases should never appear in a conclusion: "accept H0," "prove H0," or "prove Ha." H0 is either rejected, with evidence against it, or not rejected, with insufficient evidence against it. Ha is either supported by convincing evidence or it is not. This connects directly back to interpreting p-values: a large p-value never proves the null hypothesis, it only fails to contradict it, so conclusions should always be phrased in terms of evidence, never in terms of proof. A good habit is to read a finished conclusion sentence back and check that it hits all three parts, the numeric comparison of p to alpha, the formal decision, and the real-world variable stated in its original units. If any one of the three is missing, the conclusion is incomplete.
